item.title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
item.dc:creator: Tala Qraitem
item.description: Standard Bank Group automated the evidence behind its generative AI approval gates. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank built an assessment in its own AWS account that scores each use case against international AI standards and its own policies using LLM-as-a-judge on Amazon Bedrock, giving risk committees consistent, traceable evidence.
item.content:encoded:
This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group

Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline.

Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs.

Governing AI with the framework you already have

Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live.

Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar.

“At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.”

— Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group

The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases.

How the assessment works

Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria.

With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline.

Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them.

Step 1: A pre-assessment agent collects the evidence

The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find.

Step 2: The pipeline examines the artifacts and tests the application

The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence.

  • System documentation, which describes how the application was designed, built, and evaluated.
  • Policy documents, which set out roles, responsibilities, and procedures such as incident handling.
  • Source code and the system prompt, which show how controls are implemented.
  • Live calls to the application, which show how it behaves in practice.

For documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported.

For live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated.

Step 3: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation against standards

In this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no.

Every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table:

Dimension What the assessment looks for
Veracity and robustness Correct outputs, even with unexpected or adversarial inputs
Privacy and security Appropriate collection, use, and protection of data and models
Transparency Information that helps stakeholders make informed choices about their use of an AI system
Fairness Consideration of impacts on different groups of stakeholders
Safety Prevention of harmful output and misuse
Controllability Mechanisms to monitor and steer system behavior
Governance Best practices across the AI supply chain, including providers and deployers
Explainability Ways to understand and evaluate system outputs

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix.

Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix

Standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model.

The assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached.

Step 4: Reports for each audience

The pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time. Before a gate decision, reviewers confirm findings in a custom review interface with single sign-on. There they can add the use case, review the questions, amend answers with a business justification, and rewrite the output.

The assessment produces evidence against controls. It doesn’t certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations.

Testing against Standard Bank Group’s own rules

International standards give every use case a common baseline, but the bank’s risk committees approve use cases against its own policy. A question factory addresses this by generating extra judge questions from internal documents. Standard Bank Group’s risk team used it to turn internal policies into checks that run on every use case.

Because those checks are derived directly from policy language, a policy change becomes a test change. Every subsequent assessment applies the updated rule automatically, with minimal manual rework by the risk team.

“Most organizations treat policy as something you read. Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. When every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test. That fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.”

— Sri Elaprolu, Director, Frontier AI Science & Engineering, AWS

Built into the use case lifecycle

The assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle. During a proof of concept, it is optional, giving teams an early view of potential gaps. At the build stage, it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group’s production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live. After live workloads are connected, the assessment will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes, keeping the evidence current well beyond launch. The bank’s teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow.

What this means for financial institutions

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation. This strengthens responsible AI governance, reduces compliance bottlenecks, and shortens the path from assessment to production.

This approach can benefit three groups involved in approving AI use cases:

  • Risk and compliance leaders get evidence in the same format for every use case, traceable to a published standard or an internal policy clause. Start from the framework you already run, as Standard Bank Group did with its existing risk processes and approval gates.
  • Delivery teams learn what to fix during the proof of concept, when changes cost the least, instead of meeting a rejection at the approval gate.
  • Executives can grow the AI portfolio without growing the review effort at the same rate.

“Adoption of AI at scale across the enterprise requires trust, both internally and with our customers. This assessment is proving key in enabling all our product teams to demonstrate that they are building enterprise-grade solutions aligned with both our own and industry best practices.”

— Duncan Macdonald, Chief Technology Officer, Standard Bank Group

From approval gates to continuous assurance

Banks designed approval gates for systems that changed a few times a year. Generative AI applications change with every prompt update, model version, and new data source. As they take on more autonomous tasks, the number of decisions that need evidence keeps growing. Adding reviewers can’t keep pace with that rate of change.

Standard Bank Group’s approach points to a different operating model. When policies become tests and evidence is collected automatically, governance moves out of a checkpoint at the end of delivery and into the system itself. Every AI application in the portfolio can carry a current, auditable record of how it meets the bank’s standards, refreshed whenever its code or configuration changes. Risk teams spend their time on judgment calls and policy design, and the bank can show regulators the same evidence it uses for its own decisions.

The same foundation extends further. Continuous reassessment keeps evidence aligned with a changing code base after launch. New regulations can be encoded once as checks and applied across every use case. Aggregated scores give boards an enterprise-wide view of AI risk instead of a collection of individual reviews.

For any institution scaling AI, the question worth asking is how many of its policies have ever been tested against a running system. To explore how AWS Professional Services can help your organization automate AI risk assessment, contact your AWS account team. To learn more about building AI responsibly on AWS, visit Responsible AI on AWS.

About the authors

Tala Qraitem

Tala is a Senior Security Consultant with AWS Professional Services. They help financial institutions move AI systems into production safely by turning regulation and internal policy into controls that risk teams can test. Tala led the responsible AI workstream with Standard Bank Group and is the security lead for the assessment capability described in this post. They worked alongside the bank’s risk and delivery teams to build the assessment into how the bank approves new AI use cases.

Jörg Fischer

Jörg is Group Chief Information and AI Officer at Standard Bank Group, where he is also responsible for Group Real Estate Services across 20 countries. Since joining the bank in 1997, he has held senior roles in finance, technology, operations, and shared services. He has led change programs that include implementing new core banking systems and consolidating processing centers. A Chartered Accountant (SA), Jörg won CIO of the Year at the 2023 South African CIO Awards.

item.title: Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents
item.dc:creator: Keith Mascarenhas
item.description: Announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract. Describe the fields you need in natural language, submit a document or a mixed packet, and receive structured results with a confidence score and page-level grounding for each value, with no model training required.
item.content:encoded:
Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required.

The challenge of extracting data from mixed packets

Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file.

Teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate.

Amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs.

How Amazon Textract Insights works

With Amazon Textract Insights, you define what to extract in a blueprint. A blueprint is a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description of what to find. Each field also has an inference type that determines whether the value is read verbatim from the page or inferred from the content of the document. You can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. You can also author your own blueprint for the documents specific to your business.

For a mixed packet, you add the blueprints for each document type you expect to the same project. You then submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and enable splitting. Amazon Textract Insights splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each one to the blueprint that fits it, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value.

For example, suppose you receive a mortgage application as a single 26-page PDF that contains a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer’s handwritten notes. You create an Amazon Textract Insights project with the AWS public W-2, payslip, and bank statement blueprints, add a custom blueprint for loan officer notes, and enable splitting. You then submit the file from your Amazon S3 bucket with a single StartDocumentInsights call. Amazon Textract Insights splits the file into its individual documents, matches each one to its blueprint, and writes the results to your S3 bucket. Each value includes a confidence score and the page and bounding box it was drawn from.

Confidence and grounding for auditable automation

Amazon Textract Insights returns two kinds of fields: The first are explicit fields read directly from the page. The second are inferred fields derived from the document’s content. Both return with a confidence score and with grounding that identifies the page and the coordinates the value was drawn from.

Because each value is traceable to its source, a reviewer or an auditor can confirm any result against the original document. You can extend automation to documents that would previously have gone to manual review, while keeping people in the process wherever judgment is required.

“We evaluated Amazon Textract Insights and are excited about its potential. Our medical bills and forms are received from a wide variety of sources and often have different layouts and formats. As a result, extraction rules developed for one source do not always transfer effectively to another.

With Amazon Textract Insights, we can describe the fields we need in plain language, and the service identifies and extracts the corresponding data. Each extracted value is returned with a confidence score, allowing our team to focus their review efforts only on the fields where the service has lower confidence. We are also excited to explore the document splitting capabilities, which could help automatically separate multi-document files into individual documents and further streamline our document processing workflow.”

— Vijay Agrawal, Vice President, Information Systems, Symbeo, A CorVel Company

Built on the Amazon Textract engine

We updated Amazon Textract’s reading engine, Amazon Textract Core, improving accuracy, strengthening the handling of dense tables and handwriting, and expanding language coverage to 40 languages for the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs. All these benefits are available to Amazon Textract customers today with no changes. Your Amazon Textract APIs remain unchanged.

Amazon Textract Core is now generally available in two additional AWS Regions, Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich), bringing in-region processing to a total of 18 AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights isn’t yet available in these AWS Regions.

Security and data handling

Projects and blueprints

Amazon Textract Insights encrypts projects and blueprints at rest with AWS owned keys. To use your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, specify it in EncryptionConfiguration when you call CreateProject or CreateBlueprint.

Insight analysis jobs

Amazon Textract Insights reads documents from, and writes results to, the Amazon S3 buckets specified in your StartDocumentInsights request. Intermediate job data is encrypted at rest with AWS owned keys. If you specify a customer managed key in the request’s EncryptionConfiguration, Amazon Textract Insights uses it to encrypt the job’s intermediate data. All intermediate data is transient and is deleted when the job completes. Your output bucket’s default encryption applies to the results written to your bucket when the job completes. A project’s key does not apply to its jobs.

If you disable your key or remove Amazon Textract’s access to it, Amazon Textract Insights can no longer use data encrypted under it.

Cross-Region inference

Amazon Textract Insights automatically selects the optimal AWS Region within your geography to process your inference requests. This maximizes available compute resources and model availability, and is designed to deliver a consistent customer experience. All data is transmitted encrypted across Amazon’s secure network. Amazon Textract Insights securely routes your inference requests to available compute resources within the geographic area where the request originated. For example, inference requests originating in the United States are processed within the United States. Amazon Textract Core APIs are unchanged and continue to process requests in the AWS Region you call. For the list of destination AWS Regions, see the Amazon Textract documentation guide.

Getting started

Getting started with Amazon Textract Insights takes four steps.

Define what you need: Start from an AWS public blueprint or describe your own fields in natural language.

Create a project: Add your blueprints to it.

Submit your documents: Send a single document or a mixed packet from your Amazon S3 bucket with one API call.

Review the results: Accept values that meet your confidence threshold and route the rest for review. Tune your threshold on a representative sample of your own documents.

Amazon Textract Insights supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, and TIFF inputs and processes documents in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. It is priced per page rather than per token, with no minimum commitment. For current rates across Amazon Textract, see the Amazon Textract pricing page.

Conclusion

Intelligent document processing has long forced a choice between how far you can automate and how well you can audit the result. Amazon Textract Insights narrows that trade-off so your team can decide where to automate based on evidence rather than guesswork. Learn more about getting started with Amazon Textract Insights.

Visit the Amazon Textract product page.

Follow the Amazon Textract Developer Guide to author a blueprint or start with an AWS blueprint.

Register for Accelerate intelligent document processing with Amazon Textract session at re:Invent.

About the authors

Keith Mascarenhas

Keith leads worldwide go-to-market strategy for generative AI at AWS, focused on intelligent document processing and computer vision across AWS AI services and Amazon Bedrock. Since joining AWS, he has worked across product management, solutions architecture and go-to-market, giving him a builder’s view of how AI delivers business value.

Sneha Choudhury

Sneha is a Principal Product Manager driving product strategy and roadmap for AWS’s Documents & Visual AI initiatives. She shapes how AI-powered products are built and delivered to AWS customers.

Niklas Breuer

Niklas is a Sr Product Manager on the AGI team, where he defines and delivers AI-driven information products for AWS. He works closely with customers, engineering, and science teams to shape how AWS AI services are built and brought to market.

Wrick Talukdar

Wrick is a Tech Lead focusing on generative AI at Amazon Web Services, driving innovation through multimodal AI, agentic solutions, and foundational models. He is also the author of the bestselling book “Building Agentic AI Systems” and “Generative AI Ethics, Privacy, and Security” for Large Language Models. He is a keynote speaker and often presents his innovations and solutions at leading global forums, including AWS re:Invent, ICCE, Global Consumer Technology conference, and major industry events such as World Technology Summit, CERAWeek and ADIPEC. In his free time, he enjoys writing and birding photography.

Malena Lopez-Sotelo

item.title: Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
item.dc:creator: Mijanur Palash
item.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now offers enhanced observability to help you diagnose GPU training issues faster. It brings together diagnostic and profiling capabilities for training workloads on both Amazon EKS and Slurm orchestrators, pinpointing issues across GPU, network, and host layers.
item.content:encoded:
Large-scale model training is one of the most expensive workloads you can run on GPUs, and a single unhealthy accelerator can stall an entire distributed job. When training throughput drops, the hard part is rarely noticing that something is wrong. It is figuring out why and where. Teams often spend hours or days sifting through logs and disconnected dashboards to decide whether a slowdown came from a throttled GPU, a saturated network link, or a stalled data pipeline on the host.

Today, we are announcing enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a new capability that helps you diagnose GPU training issues faster. It brings together diagnostic and profiling capabilities for training workloads that run on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators:

Diagnostic summary uses Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock, and flags GPUs that deviate from their peers. Static diagnostic rules surface common failure patterns such as GPU hardware faults (XID errors, ECC memory errors), EFA throughput drops, thermal throttling, and overheating, so you catch degradation before it affects training.

Why you need it

Distributed training is expensive, and small inefficiencies compound into significant wasted GPU hours. Until now, getting visibility into HyperPod infrastructure meant stitching together separate tools, and even then, the metrics told you that performance had degraded without telling you why.

Enhanced observability closes three gaps. It isolates a single bad accelerator across hundreds or thousands of GPUs whether through XID errors, ECC memory faults, or thermal throttling, so you spend time on the fix instead of the search.

Together, these capabilities reduce troubleshooting time and help you keep expensive accelerators busy.

How it works

Each capability targets a different layer of a distributed training job.

Default and advanced metrics

Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two levels:

Default metrics (enabled automatically) cover cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. These metrics are collected every 30 seconds and sent to your chosen metric store with approximately 1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB of memory.

Advanced metrics (opt-in) provide deeper visibility:

  • Full node exporter suite: comprehensive host-level metrics.
  • All NVIDIA GPU DCGM and AWS Neuron metrics: detailed accelerator telemetry including clock speeds, power, PCIe activity, and error indicators.
  • Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) metrics: network interface throughput, drops, retransmissions, and errors.

Advanced metrics are optional because they increase the volume of telemetry sent to your metric store, which has a cost implication. Most customers running small jobs on small clusters may not need them, but they are essential for long-running training jobs on large clusters where patterns emerge over time.

Metric stores

You can choose between two metric stores:

  • Amazon CloudWatch (new default) provides native monitoring through CloudWatch SageMaker Insights, so you can visualize metrics without leaving the AWS Management Console.
  • Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus for teams that standardize on Prometheus and Grafana for observability.

Previously, only Prometheus was supported. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Amazon Managed Service Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console.

Diagnostic summary

The diagnostic summary uses two complementary approaches to surface issues across your HyperPod cluster.

GPU outlier detection uses CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare GPUs within a training job across utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, and SM clock frequency. When a GPU deviates significantly from its peers, it appears as an outlier card in the diagnostic summary. This works for both EKS and Slurm jobs.

Static diagnostic rules evaluate known failure patterns and organize detected issues by type:

  • Hardware: GPU ECC memory errors, XID faults, accelerator failures.
  • Network: EFA throughput degradation, packet drops, retransmissions.
  • Throttling: GPU clock throttling because of heat, board, or reliability limits.
  • Overheating: GPU temperatures exceeding configured limits.

Each detected issue identifies the affected job, cluster, node, accelerator, and rank.

How to get started

Enhanced observability is delivered as an add-on for EKS-orchestrated clusters and as an extension for Slurm-orchestrated clusters, which means you control who can install or change it through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).

Step 1: Create a SageMaker HyperPod cluster

If you already have a cluster, you can use it. To create a new SageMaker HyperPod cluster, you can follow the step-by-step outline. In general, the steps are as follows:

  1. On the Amazon SageMaker AI console, choose HyperPod clusters in the navigation pane.
  2. Choose Create HyperPod cluster and Orchestrated on Amazon EKS or Orchestrated by Slurm.
  3. For Setup options, select Custom setup.
  4. For Name, enter a name.
  5. For Instance recovery, select Automatic.
  6. Choose Submit.

The following screenshot shows the Create HyperPod cluster page.

Figure 1: Creating a HyperPod cluster on Amazon EKS with Custom setup

Step 2: Configure HyperPod observability

In the Custom setup workflow, expand the HyperPod observability section:

  1. Enable HyperPod Observability is checked by default. Uncheck only if you do not want observability.
  2. Observability metrics show default metrics (cluster health, CPU/disk/OS, GPU utilization/temperature, per-job resources) plus optional advanced metrics.
  3. Select advanced metrics as needed: Full node exporter suite, All NVIDIA GPU DCGM/Neuron metrics and EFA metrics.
  4. Enable logging to create CloudWatch log groups for containers and pod logs.
  5. For Metric store, choose Amazon CloudWatch (default) or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus.
  6. For Grafana workspace, choose to create a new workspace, use an existing one, or select None.
  7. Configure IAM roles or let the console create them automatically.

The following figure shows the configuration options for HyperPod observability in the custom setup path:

Figure 2: The HyperPod observability section showing default and advanced metrics, metric store (CloudWatch or Prometheus), and Grafana workspace

Note: In Quick setup, HyperPod observability is enabled by default and cannot be unchecked. Custom setup gives you control over which metric categories and advanced metrics to enable.

Step 3: Install the observability add-on using the CLI (alternative, EKS)

You can install the HyperPod observability add-on (EKS) or extension (Slurm) from the AWS Management Console or through the API. Alternatively, you can install the add-on with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

The following command creates the add-on, enables the basic metric categories and leaves the opt-in profiling capabilities off:

aws eks create-addon \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --addon-name amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-observability \
    --region <region> \
    --configuration-values '{
        "metricsDestination": "cloudwatch",
        "metricsProvider": {
            "nodeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "scrapeInterval": 30},
            "acceleratedComputeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "scrapeInterval": 30}
        },
        "profilesProvider": {
            "hostProfiling": {"enabled": false}
        }
    }'

Verify the add-on is ACTIVE:

aws eks describe-addon \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --addon-name amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-observability \
    --region <region> \
    --query 'addon.status'

The following figure shows the observability add-on on the cluster’s Add-ons tab.

Figure 3: The observability add-on on the cluster’s Add-ons tab, active and sending metrics to Amazon CloudWatch

Step 4: Enable metrics (EKS)

You can enable or disable any metric category or profiling capability at any time. For an EKS cluster, update the add-on configuration with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The following command turns on advanced network (EFA) metrics:

aws eks update-addon \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --addon-name amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-observability \
    --region <region> \
    --configuration-values '{
        "metricsDestination": "cloudwatch",
        "metricsProvider": {
            "nodeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "scrapeInterval": 30},
            "acceleratedComputeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "scrapeInterval": 30},
            "networkMetrics": {"level": "ADVANCED", "scrapeInterval": 30}
        }
    }'

From the console, choose Actions, then Edit on the add-on card to make the same changes. The following figure shows the Actions button.

Figure 4: Use Actions → Edit to enable or disable metric categories and profiling

Slurm clusters: install or edit the observability extension

On Slurm-orchestrated clusters, HyperPod observability is a cluster extension. From the cluster detail page, open the Extensions tab. If the extension is installed, choose Actions, then Edit. The following figure shows the observability extension on a Slurm cluster’s Extensions tab.

Figure 5: The observability extension on a Slurm cluster’s Extensions tab, with Actions → Edit

The edit page sets a collection level for each metric category.

Figure 6: Editing observability on a Slurm cluster: metric categories, host profiling, and the metric store

To install the extension with the AWS CLI instead:

aws sagemaker create-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn <cluster-arn> \
    --extension-name sagemaker-observability \
    --region <region> \
    --configuration-values '{
        "metricsProvider": {
            "clusterMetrics": {"level": "ENABLED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "nodeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "acceleratedComputeMetrics": {"level": "BASIC", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "jobMetrics": {"level": "ENABLED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30}
        },
        "profilesProvider": {"hostProfiling": {"enabled": false}}
    }'

To turn on EFA metrics, update the extension:

aws sagemaker update-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn <cluster-arn> \
    --extension-arn <extension-arn> \
    --region <region> \
    --configuration-values '{
        "metricsProvider": {
            "clusterMetrics": {"level": "ENABLED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "nodeMetrics": {"level": "ADVANCED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "acceleratedComputeMetrics": {"level": "ADVANCED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "networkMetrics": {"level": "ENABLED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30},
            "jobMetrics": {"level": "ENABLED", "collectionIntervalSeconds": 30}
        }
    }'

Check the status with aws sagemaker describe-cluster-extension --cluster-arn <cluster-arn> --extension-arn <extension-arn>.

Step 5: Confirm metrics are streaming

After the cluster is ready, navigate to the cluster’s detail page. The new Observability tab displays an overview with:

  • Nodes: total node count (for example, 128).
  • Accelerators: total GPU/accelerator count (for example, 1024).
  • Jobs: active and recent training job count.
  • Avg. GPU utilization: fleet-wide average (for example, 87.3%).
  • Avg. vCPU utilization: fleet-wide average (for example, 76.8%).
  • Avg. memory utilization: fleet-wide average (for example, 83.5%).

The following image shows the Cluster Observability tab with overview metrics, active and recent training jobs, and active issues:

Figure 7: The new Observability tab — fleet overview, active training jobs, and detected issues

CloudWatch dashboard

From the Observability tab, choose Open dashboard to navigate to the CloudWatch SageMaker Insights experience. The dashboard provides several views:

Diagnostic summary

The Diagnostic summary shows incidents detected across your HyperPod clusters. Pinpoint the root cause whether it is a hardware fault, a network issue, throttling, or overheating.

Choose any incident card to see more details. Each card names the affected job, cluster, accelerator, and rank.

The following screenshot shows the Diagnostic summary tab:

Figure 8: Diagnostic summary where each incident card names the job, cluster, accelerator, and issue type, with a cross-layer explanation

The following figure shows an incident detail:

Figure 9: Incident detail showing the affected job, cluster, instance, and accelerator, with evidence charts against the fleet average

Hardware tab

The Hardware tab gives a device-level view of your accelerator fleet. The fleet topology map shows every device’s state (Active, Idle, and Unhealthy). The device table lists the accelerator type, owning team, utilization, temperature, EFA usage, status, and the workload running on each device. You can search and filter by status, accelerator, or team to find an unhealthy device quickly.

The following screenshot shows the Hardware tab:

Figure 10: Hardware tab showing fleet topology and per-device accelerator, team, utilization, temperature, EFA, status, and workload

Workload tab

The Workload tab lists active and recent training jobs with their type (for example, distributed training, fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning), status, and duration. It also shows resource usage per job: EFA, GPU and CPU utilization, and memory. The tab flags jobs with abnormal network usage.

The following screenshot shows the Workload tab:

Figure 11: Workload tab showing training jobs with per-job EFA, GPU, CPU, and memory usage

You can select a job to view more details. The following screenshot shows the job detail view:

Figure 12: Job detail showing accelerator metrics

The Network tab

The Network tab summarizes the health of the inter-node communication fabric for distributed workloads. Overview metrics include fleet-average EFA utilization, degraded node count, and retransmits. A breakdown by instance type shows the share of healthy and degraded nodes for each.

The following screenshot shows the Network tab:

Figure 13: Network tab showing fabric overview and EFA health by instance type

Amazon Managed Grafana dashboard

From the cluster Observability tab or the Add-ons page, choose Open dashboard in Grafana to access prebuilt Amazon Managed Grafana dashboards. These dashboards give you full-stack visibility into HyperPod clusters, with telemetry from CloudWatch or Prometheus visualized across cluster, node, GPU, network, and job dimensions.

Note: If using Grafana for the first time, you must first configure AWS IAM Identity Center and add Grafana users. Documentation links are provided during cluster creation when you select the Grafana metric store option.

The following screenshot shows a prebuilt Grafana dashboard:

Figure 14: Prebuilt Grafana dashboard showing GPU performance metrics per node and GPU

Now available

Enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available today in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Learn more:

  • For pricing information and a list of supported cluster instance types, see Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.
  • Check out the Developer Guide.
  • Visit the AWS Management Console to start training with the enhanced observability add-on.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
item.dc:creator: Aryaman Kothari
item.description: This second installment reviews 13 more Amazon SageMaker AI inference launches from 2026, spanning configuration recommendations, fitting more models onto each GPU, serving models too large for one instance, cross-Region routing, and post-launch tuning, bringing the year's total to 26.
item.content:encoded:
From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more launches for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference

In September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint. Most of them answered one question: how do I get this model serving quickly and reliably? This post covers the 13 launches that came next, bringing the total for 2026 to 26.

Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.

For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway and the Global Inference Gateway deliver the routing and multi-Region work, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.

To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.

The launches at a glance

Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the launches in each

Choose the right configuration from wherever you work

The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.

Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.

Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026)

Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI

The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.

SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.

Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026)

Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK

Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.

The SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.

LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026)

Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters

Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.

Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, update, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.

SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026)

Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI

Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.

Inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (feasible_max) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (infeasible_min).

The search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (concurrency_min, concurrency_max, search_max_iterations, and search_initial_points) bound the cost and speed up convergence.

Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026)

Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent

Engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.

The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:

  • Find the right instance. Ranked deployment options with measured throughput, latency, and TTFT for a model in Amazon S3, SageMaker JumpStart, or the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Benchmark a live endpoint. A report from real load covering throughput, P50 and P99 latency, inter-token latency, and supported concurrency.
  • Compare runs. The percentage change on every metric, which shows whether a configuration change helped.

Answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.

For the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.

Fit more models onto each GPU

The support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.

Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026)

Developer guide: Inference Components in the SageMaker AI Console

With Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.

In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, update, and delete inference components:

  • Create and edit. Create an endpoint with inference components, add or delete components later, and change each component’s accelerators, CPU, memory, and copy count.
  • Scale each model. Set an automatic scaling policy for each component, down to zero copies, so an idle model stops holding accelerators.
  • Monitor. See alarms and per-component metrics on the same page.

The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.

GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (October 2026)

Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.

MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.

Figure 2: Three small models on three GPUs, compared with the same models in partitions of one GPU

For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.

Serve models larger than one instance

The team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.

Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026)

Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.

With this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:

  • Capacity and networking. GPU capacity and EFA networking, provisioned and wired automatically.
  • Node recovery. Node health monitoring and replacement, with multi-node workers rescheduled automatically when a node fails.
  • Endpoint operations. Autoscaling, endpoint registration, TLS, and observability.
  • One install and upgrade path. The Inference Operator add-on installs Dynamo, the serving images, and the Grove and KAI schedulers as one unit and upgrades them together.

The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:

  • Multi-node (sharded) serving. One copy of the model spans several nodes, so you can serve models that do not fit on any single instance.
  • Disaggregated prefill and decode. Prompt processing and token generation run on separate GPU pools, each on an instance type suited to its work, so a long prompt no longer slows responses for other users.
  • KV-aware routing. Each request goes to the worker that already holds its KV cache, which reduces TTFT.

There are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can update the add-on and add a short dynamoSpec block to an existing InferenceEndpointConfig, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.

Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Figure 3: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference

For the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.

Send each request to a GPU that can serve it

The support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.

Routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the launches below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.

Figure 4: Routing across Regions and inside each endpoint or cluster, on both deployment paths

KV-cache-aware routing for endpoints (November 2026)

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

Applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.

KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.

It works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.

Which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over quickly.

Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026)

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway

Inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, new requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.

The Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:

  • KV cache utilization. Avoids pods whose cache is nearly full.
  • Queue depth and running requests. Avoids pods with a backlog and balances active work.
  • Prefix cache hit rate. Prefers pods likely to hold the prompt prefix.
  • LoRA adapter residency. Prefers pods that already hold the requested adapter, which avoids swap latency.

Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Global Inference Gateway for HyperPod (November 2026)

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway

The Inference Gateway routes within a cluster, and each cluster can serve only the requests sent to it. A request can wait on a saturated cluster in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another. Clients had to choose a cluster themselves, and when a cluster failed, an engineer had to move traffic by hand.

The Global Inference Gateway gives teams one SageMaker-managed endpoint across every cluster they register. For each request, it scores clusters on queue depth, free KV cache, proximity to the caller, and recent error rate, and sends the request to the best one over the AWS private backbone. The Inference Gateway in that cluster still picks the pod. Requests authenticate with SigV4 and IAM. When a cluster becomes saturated or unhealthy, traffic shifts to the next-best cluster in under 30 seconds with no action from the client, and the cluster rejoins the pool when it recovers. Routing weights are tunable, with defaults if you leave them unset.

Adding or removing a model or cluster does not change anything for the applications that call the endpoint. No cluster is reachable until you publish it, and the published resources stay in your account. The Global Inference Gateway is available in the Regions listed in the AWS documentation.

Cross-Region Inference Routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

Blog: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

On managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.

The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:

  • One invocation path. SageMaker tries the local endpoint first and moves traffic to another registered endpoint when the local one cannot serve a request.
  • One routing policy. The policy combines endpoint metrics with service-side capacity signals, including insufficient capacity errors that customers cannot observe on their own.
  • Private connectivity. Cross-Region traffic runs over AWS PrivateLink with a managed cross-account authorization model, so routing to another Region or account does not need internet or NAT gateways.
  • Overflow and residency guardrails. The endpoint owner can cap how much cross-Region traffic a fallback endpoint accepts, and the application can restrict which Regions may serve a request.

Figure 5: Cross-Region Inference Router request flow

The two cross-Region launches apply the same idea on each deployment path. The team keeps ownership of its clusters and endpoints, and SageMaker supplies the routing, the private connectivity, and the failover.

Global Inference Gateway Cross-Region Inference Router
Deployment path HyperPod Inference Managed endpoints
Routes across Registered HyperPod clusters in any Region Registered Regional endpoints, across Regions and accounts
Connectivity AWS private backbone, SigV4 and IAM AWS PrivateLink, managed cross-account authorization
Failover Automatic, in under 30 seconds Automatic, when the local endpoint cannot serve
Owner controls A cluster is reachable only after you publish it Overflow caps per fallback endpoint and Region restrictions per application

For the support team, the US morning peak now overflows to capacity in Europe on both paths, and requests that must stay in Europe are restricted to European Regions in the router policy.

Keep endpoints tuned after launch

Two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.

Continuous performance monitoring (November 2026)

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints

Amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.

There are three types of findings:

  • Latency drift after a traffic change. When a change such as added retrieval lengthens prompts, TTFT rises. The finding quantifies the regression week over week and recommends re-running inference recommendations against recent traffic to find a configuration that brings TTFT back down.
  • A configuration gap present since deployment. The endpoint was never well tuned for its workload, and the finding points to the change that would close the gap.
  • Idle GPU capacity. When capacity stays unused week after week, the finding flags a chance to right-size the endpoint and reduce cost.

In-place rolling model updates (November 2026)

A standard rolling update replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding new capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.

SageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The update still rolls out in stages, but it needs new capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.

Figure 6: A rolling update acquires new instances at every step. An in-place rolling update acquires one batch at the start and reuses the rest of the fleet

For the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a new recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.

Summary: 14 launches, continuing from part 1

The numbering continues from the 13 launches in part 1.

14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.

15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.

16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.

17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.

18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.

19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.

20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.

21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.

22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.

23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.

24. Global Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint across clusters and Regions, with failover in under 2 minutes.

25. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.

26. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.

27. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.

By the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.

Part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 13 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.

What is next

On managed endpoints, we plan to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model update.

Documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.
